title: Bring Your Own Expert! Extending MoE Models with New Domain Expertise
gist: TNG shows that a frozen MoE model (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base) can be extended with independently trained, drop-in domain experts (Rust +11 pts, Haskell +19 pts pass@1) without general-capability regression, and that these experts compose by simple concatenation where merged LoRA adapters collapse. The pitch is an ecosystem of swappable domain experts on a fixed base model, with inference-efficiency and post-training robustness still open.

themes.theme: Drop-in experts for frozen MoE models

insights.claim: TNG extended Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base with newly trained Rust and Haskell experts, improving language-specific benchmarks with no drop in baseline capabilities.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Shows open-weight MoE models can be cheaply specialized post hoc, lowering the barrier for domain-specific model vendors.

insights.claim: In TNG's expert-extension method the base MoE weights stay frozen and only the added experts plus their router rows are trained, about 125 million parameters per expert on a 35-billion-parameter model.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Training a tiny fraction of parameters cuts the compute cost of adding a domain capability to a large model.
insights.quote: roughly 125 million parameters per expert on our 35 billion parameter test model

insights.claim: New experts compete with base experts for tokens via the router, so tokens outside the new domain are routed to the original experts and the base model behaves almost exactly as before.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Router-gated specialization is a mechanism for adding capability without regression risk, a key concern for enterprise deployment.
insights.locator: By training the new router rows

insights.claim: TNG solves the cold-start problem of new MoE experts by initializing each new expert and router row from the most active existing expert in that layer and briefly freezing the router so the router does not switch the new expert off.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: A reusable training recipe that makes expert grafting practical for other labs and fine-tuning vendors.
insights.locator: A key practical challenge is the cold-start problem

insights.claim: After training, the new expert weights are concatenated onto the base model's expert tensors, producing a standard Hugging Face checkpoint that needs only a configuration change and no custom inference code.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: No custom serving stack is needed, so grafted-expert models can run on existing inference infrastructure.
insights.quote: This is just a configuration change and does not need custom inference code.
insights.locator: After training, the new expert weights

insights.claim: A grafted Rust expert raised Rust code generation pass@1 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base from 0.62 to 0.73, while a Haskell expert raised Haskell pass@1 from 0.32 to 0.51.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Gains of 11 and 19 points show the largest uplift in weaker, lower-resource domains where base models underperform.

insights.claim: On a seven-task general suite (ARC Easy/Challenge, BoolQ, HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande), the Rust- and Haskell-extended models scored 0.78 and 0.80 against the base model's 0.80, within noise.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Domain specialization via added experts appears close to free in terms of general capability.
insights.quote: The new capabilities come at no cost to existing ones.

insights.claim: Training new experts for a single domain took roughly half a day on one 8-GPU NVIDIA B200 node using NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel on The Stack v1 data.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Half a day on one node puts domain-expert creation within reach of small teams, widening the market for specialized open models.
insights.quote: Training new experts for a single domain takes roughly half a day.

insights.claim: Independently trained Rust and Haskell experts combined into one checkpoint retained both gains, scoring 0.70 on Rust and 0.50 on Haskell pass@1 with general capability at baseline.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Composable experts enable mix-and-match model products assembled from separately trained modules.

insights.claim: A brief retraining of only the new router rows on 50/50 Rust and Haskell data fully restored Rust and baseline scores and could surpass the single-expert Haskell score, without retraining the experts.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Cheap router-only rebalancing makes combining many domain modules operationally light.
insights.locator: Then, we did a brief retraining

insights.claim: Independently trained LoRA adapters interfere when combined because they modify the same shared weights: averaging the Rust and Haskell adapters collapsed scores to 0.67 Rust and 0.36 Haskell, and summing them did worse than the base model on Rust.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Challenges the default LoRA-adapter ecosystem for multi-domain customization and favors MoE-native modular approaches.
insights.quote: Neither LoRA merge maintains both domains simultaneously.

insights.claim: Single-domain LoRA adapters performed similarly to added experts (0.74 Rust, 0.48 Haskell), so the expert approach's advantage lies in composition rather than single-domain quality.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: LoRA remains adequate for single-domain fine-tuning; the differentiator only matters for multi-domain products.
insights.locator: For comparison, we fine-tuned LoRA adapters

insights.claim: Grafted MoE experts compose by construction because they live in a disjoint parameter space, so combining them is simply concatenation.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Parameter isolation is the design principle to watch for modular, upgradable model architectures.

themes.theme: Vision of a composable expert ecosystem

insights.claim: TNG envisions an ecosystem of a frozen, capable base model plus a growing library of drop-in domain experts that can be added, exchanged, or removed on demand without retraining the base.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Could create a marketplace for third-party domain experts on top of open MoE base models, analogous to plugin ecosystems.
insights.quote: a frozen, capable base model, plus a growing library of drop-in domain experts

insights.claim: Work from the Allen Institute for AI earlier in 2026 showed domain-specific experts in MoE models are possible and practical, though pretraining-emergent experts normally do not specialize in human-recognizable domains.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Signals converging research interest in controllable MoE modularity across labs.

insights.claim: Simply appending experts to an MoE model may harm inference efficiency by breaking expert parallelism across GPUs and expert load-balancing, which TNG suggests could be mitigated by pruning dispensable experts with techniques such as REAP.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Serving-cost penalties could limit adoption unless expert replacement via pruning matures.

insights.claim: TNG has only tested added experts during continued pretraining on two programming languages; whether they survive a full post-training pipeline and stay modular at larger expert counts remains unproven.
insights.speaker: Fabian Klemm
insights.so_what: Treat the result as early-stage research until validated on post-trained models and non-code domains.
